clinicalPearls: More than one billion people worldwide are infected with one or more intestinal nematode species; they are most common where sanitation and fecal-waste disposal are inadequate, especially resource-limited tropical and subtropical regions, but are seen with increasing frequency among immigrants and refugees to developed countries (p.1814).

The major intestinal roundworms are Ascaris lumbricoides, the hookworms (Necator americanus, Ancylostoma duodenale, A. ceylanicum), Strongyloides stercoralis, Trichuris trichiura (whipworm), and Enterobius vermicularis (pinworm) (p.1815).
Ascaris, Trichuris, and the hookworms require a soil phase for development, whereas S. stercoralis and E. vermicularis can be transmitted directly from person to person (p.1814).

Because most helminths cannot fully complete their life cycle within the same human host, heavy adult-worm burdens require repeated exposure; clinical disease (versus asymptomatic/subclinical infection) generally develops only with repeated exposure and is typically related to infection intensity (p.1814).
Eosinophilia and elevated serum IgE are features of many helminth infections, the latter particularly when the life cycle involves tissue migration (Ascaris, Strongyloides, hookworms) (p.1814).

Ascaris larval migration through the lungs (~9-12 days after egg ingestion) can cause an irritating nonproductive cough, substernal discomfort, eosinophilia, and transient rounded pulmonary infiltrates - eosinophilic pneumonitis (Loffler's syndrome) (p.1815).

Heavy Ascaris infection can cause small-bowel obstruction by a bolus of entangled worms (more common in children with narrow lumens), sometimes complicated by perforation, intussusception, or volvulus; an adult worm migrating into the biliary tree can cause biliary colic, cholecystitis, cholangitis, pancreatitis, or rarely intrahepatic abscess (p.1815).
In highly endemic areas, intestinal and biliary ascariasis can rival acute appendicitis as a cause of surgical acute abdomen (p.1815).

The major consequence of chronic hookworm infection is iron deficiency; symptoms are minimal if iron stores are adequate, but undernourished individuals develop progressive iron-deficiency anemia and hypoproteinemia (fatigue, weakness, dyspnea). Hookworm disease requires the combination of heavy worm burden, prolonged duration, and inadequate iron intake (p.1816).

Hookworm larvae may cause a pruritic maculopapular rash (ground itch) at the skin penetration site; hypochromic microcytic anemia, sometimes with eosinophilia or hypoalbuminemia, is characteristic of hookworm disease (p.1816).

S. stercoralis is distinguished by its ability - unique among helminths except Capillaria - to complete its life cycle and replicate within a human host (autoinfection), so infection can persist for decades without further exogenous exposure (p.1816).

Larva currens, a rapidly advancing (up to ~10 cm/h) pruritic serpiginous skin eruption, is pathognomonic of strongyloidiasis; recurrent urticaria, often on the buttocks, is the most common cutaneous manifestation (p.1816).

Impaired cell-mediated immunity - especially high-dose glucocorticoid therapy, and less commonly other immunosuppressants or HTLV-1 infection - can trigger Strongyloides hyperinfection with massive larval numbers, leading to colitis/enteritis/malabsorption and disseminated disease (CNS, skin, peritoneum, liver, kidneys) (p.1817).

Disseminated strongyloidiasis is often complicated by gram-negative bacteremia, pneumonia, or meningitis from enteric flora translocating through disrupted mucosal barriers; eosinophilia is often ABSENT in severely infected patients (p.1817).

Even asymptomatic strongyloidiasis must be treated because of the potential for later hyperinfection and fatal dissemination; Strongyloides serology should be performed before starting glucocorticoids or solid-organ transplantation in patients with prior potential exposure, especially with eosinophilia (p.1817).

Most Trichuris (whipworm) infections are asymptomatic, but heavy infections may cause anemia and bloody/mucoid diarrhea resembling inflammatory bowel disease; massive infection in children can cause rectal prolapse from protracted tenesmus (p.1818).

Enterobius (pinworm) is more common in temperate climates than the tropics; perianal pruritus, worse at night when gravid females emerge, is the cardinal symptom, and eosinophilia is uncommon (p.1818).
harrison.pathophysiology: Intestinal nematodes are nonsegmented roundworms ranging from ~1 mm to many centimeters. Ascaris and the hookworms have life cycles involving migration through the heart and lungs before maturing in the intestine (larvae penetrate alveoli, ascend the bronchial tree, are swallowed, and reach the small bowel). Ascaris adults live in the small-intestinal lumen and females are extraordinarily fecund (>200,000 eggs/day); eggs are highly environmentally resistant and become infective after maturation in warm, moist soil. Hookworm adults attach to the small-bowel mucosa using buccal teeth (Ancylostoma) or cutting plates (Necator), invade submucosa, and ingest blood and villous tissue, producing iron-deficiency anemia; filariform larvae penetrate skin. S. stercoralis filariform larvae penetrate skin or mucous membranes, migrate via blood to the lungs and then the small intestine, where parthenogenetic adult females embed in the mucosa; rhabditiform larvae can transform directly into filariform larvae that re-penetrate the colonic wall or perianal skin to drive ongoing autoinfection - which can amplify into hyperinfection and dissemination under immunosuppression. Trichuris adults embed their thin anterior portions in colonic/cecal mucosa with no pulmonary larval passage. Enterobius adults dwell in the cecum; gravid females migrate nocturnally to the perianal skin to deposit eggs, which become infective within hours and spread by hand-to-mouth (autoinfection from scratching) and retroinfection. (p.1814-1818)
additionalDifferentials: Strongyloides midepigastric pain resembles peptic ulcer disease, except it is aggravated by food ingestion (p.1816)
Heavy trichuriasis with bloody/mucoid diarrhea may resemble inflammatory bowel disease (p.1818)
Intestinal/biliary ascariasis may present as a surgical acute abdomen mimicking acute appendicitis in endemic areas (p.1815)
infectionMimics: Strongyloides hyperinfection-associated gram-negative sepsis, pneumonia, or meningitis can dominate or be mistaken for primary bacterial infection (p.1817)
Hookworm rhabditiform larvae in non-fresh stool must be differentiated from Strongyloides larvae (p.1816)
nonInfectiousMimics: Acute appendicitis / surgical acute abdomen (intestinal or biliary ascariasis) (p.1815)
additionalInvestigations: Stool microscopy for characteristic ova and parasites: Ascaris eggs (~65 x 45 um), hookworm eggs (~40 x 60 um, species indistinguishable by light microscopy), Trichuris lemon-shaped eggs (~50 x 20 um) (p.1815-1818)

Strongyloides: rhabditiform larvae (~250 um, short buccal cavity) on stool microscopy; single stool detects only ~one-third of uncomplicated cases, so serial examinations and agar plate method improve sensitivity; duodenojejunal aspirate/biopsy; ELISA serum antibody serology (sensitive for uncomplicated infection); in dissemination, filariform larvae in stool, sputum, bronchoalveolar lavage, or surgical drainage fluid (p.1817)
Enterobius: eggs are NOT found in stool - diagnose with morning cellulose acetate tape applied to the perianal region (eggs oval, ~55 x 25 um, flattened on one side) (p.1818)
Ascaris lung phase: larvae detectable in sputum or gastric aspirates before eggs appear in stool; chest imaging showing transient rounded infiltrates (Loffler's syndrome) (p.1815)
PCR of stool worm DNA (increasing use, mostly research/some clinical) for species-level diagnosis (p.1815-1818)
Abdominal imaging: plain film for masses of worms in obstruction; ultrasound and ERCP for pancreaticobiliary Ascaris (ERCP can also extract worms) (p.1815)
Hookworm disease bloodwork: hypochromic microcytic anemia, sometimes eosinophilia or hypoalbuminemia (p.1816)
redFlags: Disseminated strongyloidiasis - particularly in patients with unsuspected infection who are taking glucocorticoids - has a HIGH mortality rate (p.1817)
Strongyloides hyperinfection with gram-negative sepsis, pneumonia, or meningitis from enteric flora translocation (p.1817)
Eosinophilia is often ABSENT in severe/disseminated strongyloidiasis, removing a reassuring marker (p.1817)
Complete intestinal obstruction with perforation, intussusception, or volvulus from a heavy Ascaris worm bolus (p.1815)
Biliary Ascaris causing cholangitis, pancreatitis, or intrahepatic abscess (p.1815)
harrison.prognosis: Intestinal nematode infections are not usually fatal but contribute to malnutrition, impaired physical and cognitive development, and diminished work capacity, particularly in children with marginal nutritional status. Significant protective immunity does not appear to develop in humans. The major exception is strongyloidiasis: autoinfection allows decades-long persistence, and in immunocompromised hosts hyperinfection and dissemination can be fatal (high mortality, especially with unrecognized infection on glucocorticoids). (p.1814, p.1816-1817)
pitfalls: Failing to screen for and treat asymptomatic strongyloidiasis before glucocorticoids or solid-organ transplantation - asymptomatic infection must still be treated because of the risk of later hyperinfection and fatal dissemination (p.1817)
Relying on eosinophilia to exclude strongyloidiasis - it is often absent in severe/disseminated disease (p.1817)
Using routine stool ova-and-parasite microscopy to diagnose pinworm - Enterobius eggs are not passed in feces; perianal cellulose acetate tape is required (p.1818)
Single stool examination for Strongyloides detects only about one-third of uncomplicated cases (p.1817)
Misidentifying hookworm rhabditiform larvae (in non-fresh stool) as Strongyloides (p.1816)
harrison.severityClassification: Harrison does not provide a formal severity classification for intestinal nematode infections; severity correlates with infection intensity (worm burden) and host factors. Disease ranges from asymptomatic/subclinical light infection to clinical disease with heavy burden (e.g., Ascaris bowel/biliary obstruction; hookworm iron-deficiency anemia/hypoproteinemia; Trichuris dysentery and rectal prolapse). For Strongyloides, the spectrum is uncomplicated strongyloidiasis vs. hyperinfection (amplified autoinfection, larvae confined largely to the normal migration route) vs. disseminated strongyloidiasis (larvae in CNS, skin, peritoneum, liver, kidneys). (p.1814-1817)
management: Give a benzimidazole anthelmintic (albendazole or mebendazole) for Ascaris, hookworm, whipworm and pinworm infections
Treat Strongyloides with ivermectin, using prolonged or repeated courses for hyperinfection
Correct iron-deficiency anaemia with iron supplementation in heavy hookworm infection
Treat close household contacts and reinforce hygiene, handwashing and laundering for pinworm to prevent reinfection
Screen for and treat latent Strongyloides before immunosuppression to avert hyperinfection syndrome
Manage complications such as biliary or intestinal obstruction from Ascaris by endoscopic or surgical extraction
Reinforce sanitation, safe faecal disposal and mass deworming programmes to reduce reinfection
Provide nutritional rehabilitation, particularly in children with impaired growth and cognition
